rules.title: RLCC § 9 — standard terms and the parol-evidence rule
rules.summary: A standard term that contradicts, unreasonably limits, or fails to give the effect a consumer reasonably expected to a business's earlier affirmation of fact or promise is not a final expression of the agreement on that subject, so the parol-evidence rule does not discharge the earlier affirmation or promise.
rules.notes:
Section 9 is one sentence. It works by denying the standard term the status the parol-evidence rule depends on: the term is not treated as a final expression on that subject, so there is no integration to discharge the business's prior affirmation or promise.

Comment 1 states the reason. Standard terms are not a jointly drafted memorial of a negotiated agreement, so there is less reason to let them override what the consumer was told. It describes § 9 as a corollary of § 7 (deception) and § 8 (affirmations and promises are part of the contract and cannot be negated by standard terms).

Read with Restatement (Second) §§ 209–216 and UCC § 2-202 from the same assignment: those ask whether a writing is integrated; § 9 answers that question against the business for a standard term that conflicts with its own earlier statement.

Paraphrase of the black-letter text of the Official Text (2024) on file; the comments and reporters' notes were not summarised.

rules.title: RLCC § 8 — affirmations and promises that are part of the contract
rules.summary: A business's affirmation of fact or promise that leads a consumer in its intended audience reasonably to expect the subject matter to have a particular attribute becomes part of the consumer contract, and standard terms that negate or unreasonably limit the resulting obligation are not enforceable.
rules.notes:
(a) The business's own affirmation or promise becomes part of the contract when it creates a reasonable expectation, in a consumer who is the intended audience, that the subject matter will have a particular attribute.

(b) A third party's affirmation or promise of that kind (1) becomes part of the contract between the business and the consumer if the business knew or reasonably should have known of it and the consumer could reasonably have believed the business intended to stand behind it; and (2) binds the third party itself to the consumer, even without a direct transaction, if the third party has an appreciable financial interest in the contract.

(c) Standard contract terms that purport to negate or unreasonably limit obligations arising under (a) and (b) are not enforceable.

The syllabus lists § 8 twice: with the parol-evidence rule (Assignment 13, alongside § 9) and with standard forms and adhesion (Assignment 17).

rules.title: RLCC § 6 — unconscionability
rules.summary: An unconscionable consumer contract or term is unenforceable; substantive and procedural unconscionability are weighed on a sliding scale as of the time of contracting, and a sufficiently high degree of one can be enough in appropriate circumstances.
rules.notes:
(a) An unconscionable contract or term is unenforceable.

(b) Two factors, judged when the contract is made: substantive unconscionability (a fundamentally unfair or unreasonably one-sided contract or term) and procedural unconscionability (unfair surprise, or the absence of meaningful choice for the consumer). More of one means less of the other is needed, and in appropriate circumstances a sufficiently high degree of one is sufficient.

(c) A term is substantively unconscionable if its effect is to (1) unreasonably exclude or limit the business's liability or the consumer's remedies for death or personal injury, or for loss caused by the business's intentional or negligent act or omission; (2) unreasonably expand the consumer's liability or the business's remedies or enforcement powers on the consumer's breach; or (3) unreasonably limit the consumer's ability to pursue or express a complaint or seek reasonable redress.

(d) A term is procedurally unconscionable if a reasonable consumer in the circumstances is not aware of it, or does not understand or appreciate its implications, and so does not meaningfully account for it in deciding to contract. Relevant factors: the consumer's legal and financial sophistication, the complexity of the term or agreement, pressure tactics and manipulation by the business, and the process by which the term was introduced.

rules.title: RLCC § 4 — interpretation, construction and good faith
rules.summary: A consumer contract carries a non-disclaimable duty of good faith and fair dealing; a standard term with more than one reasonable meaning is read against the business, and standard terms are interpreted to give effect to the consumer's reasonable expectations.
rules.notes:
(a) Each party owes a non-disclaimable duty of good faith and fair dealing in performance and enforcement.

(b) Among the reasonable meanings of a standard contract term, the one that operates against the business supplying it is preferred.

(c) Uncertainty in the notices that are part of the process of adopting standard terms is resolved against the business using that process.

(d) Standard contract terms are interpreted in a manner that effectuates the consumer's reasonable expectations.

Comment 1 says the section does not displace the Restatement (Second)'s interpretation rules; comment 2 ties subsection (a) to Restatement (Second) § 205 and UCC § 1-201(20). The syllabus assigns § 4 with performance in good faith (Assignment 16).

hub.title: Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts (RLCC) §§ 1–10
hub.summary: The complete Official Text (2024) of the Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts is on file ("Complete Restatement.pdf", 197 pages, §§ 1–10 with comments and reporters' notes). The syllabus assigns § 2 (Assignments 6 and 9), § 3 (11), §§ 8–9 (13), § 4 (16), § 8 (17) and § 6 (18).
hub.notes:
Each section opens at its own page from the source buttons. Sections 4, 6, 8 and 9 also have their own entries on the Contracts map, in the subtopic of the assignment that lists them.

§ 2. Adoption of standard terms (Assignments 6, 9). (a) A standard term is adopted if the business shows the consumer manifested assent to the transaction after reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review it. (b) For terms available only after assent: reasonable advance notice that terms will follow, of the opportunity to review and terminate, and that not terminating adopts them; a reasonable opportunity to review afterwards; and a reasonable opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value or personal burden, not exercised. (c) A contract is not unenforceable because some standard terms were not adopted; its terms are those adopted, any unadopted standard terms the consumer elects, terms both parties agreed to, and terms supplied by law.

§ 3. Modification of standard terms (Assignment 11). (a) In an ongoing relationship a proposed modification is adopted only if the business shows reasonable notice of the modified term and opportunity to review it; a reasonable, noticed opportunity to reject it and continue under the existing term; reasonable notice that continuing without rejecting adopts it; and either assent or continued use after the rejection period. (b) The contract may set a reasonable modification procedure, which may substitute a reasonable opportunity to terminate for the opportunity to reject, but may not otherwise exclude (a) to the consumer's detriment. (c) The modification must be proposed in good faith, be fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated at contracting, and not undermine an affirmation or promise that was part of the basis of the original bargain. (d) Standard terms may not be modified once the contract has been substantially performed by at least one party.

§ 4, § 6, § 8, § 9: see their own entries.

Not assigned, on file: § 1 (definitions and scope), § 5 (discretionary obligations), § 7 (deception), § 10 (derogation from mandatory provisions).

The 2019 Tentative Draft reprinted in the Contracts Selections is superseded by the 2024 text.
